\chapter{El plazo}
\label{ch:es-plazo}
\hlchaptermodality{458}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can deal with a deadline: read the window of dates, hand a form in the right way, and understand that nothing is accepted once the window shuts.}

Read the message or notice this chapter's words exist for, then say the same thing back.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el plazo]{el plazo — by when}

\label{lesson:ES-C458-plazo}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{el placer} and \textbf{la fecha}. One of those two is an odd relative of the word coming next.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el plazo}
\textbf{el plazo} — the period allowed, and so the deadline.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Plazo} de presentación: hasta el 30 de abril.
\end{quote}

\emph{Fuera de plazo} — past the deadline. \emph{En el plazo de diez días} — within ten days. \emph{A corto plazo} — in the short term.

A second sense on any purchase: \textbf{pagar a plazos} — to pay in instalments, each one a period agreed in advance.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: plazo is not fecha}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what it names} & \textbf{the word} \\
\midrule
a day on the calendar & \textbf{la fecha} \\
the stretch of time you are allowed & \textbf{el plazo} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{La fecha límite} is the last day; \emph{el plazo} is the whole window that ends there. So \emph{el plazo termina el viernes} and \emph{la fecha límite es el viernes} say the same thing from opposite ends — one names the run, the other the wall at the end of it.

Most official Spanish prefers \emph{plazo}, because a form cares how long you have, not which square on the calendar.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{placitum} — \textquotedblleft{}a thing agreed\textquotedblright{}, the past participle of \textbf{placēre}, to please. What pleased both parties was what they had settled on.

That makes \emph{el plazo} a relative of \textbf{el placer}, which you already have. Pleasure and a deadline sit oddly together until you see the middle step: \emph{placitum} meant an agreement, then the term of an agreement, then the time you have got.

French took the same \emph{placitum} and made \textbf{plaid}, a court hearing, and English has \textbf{plea} and \textbf{plead} from it — all of them agreements argued over. Spanish kept the calmest branch: a \emph{plazo} is what was agreed, and the paperwork holds you to it.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the deadline is the thirtieth of April
  \item past the deadline
  \item what \emph{pagar a plazos} means
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The deadline? (\textbf{El plazo}.) The date? (\textbf{La fecha}.) What did \emph{placitum} mean? (\textbf{A thing agreed}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[entregar]{entregar — hand it over}

\label{lesson:ES-C458-entregar}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{el documento} and \textbf{el almacén}. Things leave both of them the same way.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: entregar}
\textbf{entregar} — to hand in, hand over, deliver.

\emph{Entregar los papeles} — to hand the paperwork in. \emph{Hay que entregarlo antes del viernes} — it has to be in before Friday. \emph{El paquete se entrega mañana} — the parcel is delivered tomorrow.

\textbf{La entrega} is the noun: \emph{la entrega a domicilio} is home delivery, and \emph{el plazo de entrega} is the delivery time — both of this chapter's first two words in one phrase.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: entregar is not dar}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what is happening} & \textbf{the verb} \\
\midrule
passing something to somebody & \textbf{dar} \\
handing over what was owed or due & \textbf{entregar} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Dame el boli} — pass me the pen. \emph{Entrega el boli} would sound as though the pen were evidence.

\emph{Entregar} carries an obligation with it: homework, a form, a parcel, a set of keys. Something was due, and now it has gone across. That is why a courier \emph{entrega} and a friend \emph{da}.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{integrare}, to make whole — from \textbf{integer}, \textbf{untouched, complete}, which is \emph{in-} plus the root of \emph{tangere}, to touch. An \emph{integer} is a thing nobody has broken into.

So \emph{entregar} is to hand a thing over \textbf{entire} — the sense of a delivery that arrives with nothing missing.

The same \emph{integer} gave Spanish \textbf{entero}, whole, and \textbf{íntegro}, which is the bookish twin and means upright about a person. English took the number sense as \textbf{integer} and the character sense as \textbf{integrity} — and \emph{integrity} is exactly what \emph{entregar} asks for: the thing handed over undiminished.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item it has to be handed in before Friday
  \item the delivery time, using both words
  \item which verb a friend passing you a pen would use
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To hand in? (\textbf{Entregar}.) The delivery? (\textbf{La entrega}.) What did \emph{integer} mean? (\textbf{Whole, untouched}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[admitir]{admitir — let it through}

\label{lesson:ES-C458-admitir}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{meter} and \textbf{aceptar}. The word coming next is a cousin of the first and a rival of the second.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: admitir}
\textbf{admitir} — to allow in, to accept as valid, and to own up to.

\begin{quote}
No se \textbf{admiten} solicitudes fuera de plazo.
\end{quote}

\emph{No se admiten perros} — no dogs. \emph{Admitir un error} — to admit a mistake. \emph{¿Admiten tarjeta?} — do you take cards, on a sign or a form.

\textbf{La admisión} is the noun, and \emph{admitido} is the word beside your name on a list when you are in.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: admitir, aceptar, entregar}]
Three verbs about a thing crossing a line, sorted by who is doing what:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the move} & \textbf{the verb} \\
\midrule
you agree to take what is offered & \textbf{aceptar} \\
an institution lets it through & \textbf{admitir} \\
you hand over what was due & \textbf{entregar} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

You \emph{entregas} the form; the office \emph{admite} it or not; a shop \emph{acepta} your card. Notice who is behind \emph{admitir}: nearly every time, an institution. That is why it turns up in the \emph{se} form on notices — \emph{no se admiten} — with nobody named.

The other sense follows from the same picture: to \emph{admit} a mistake is to let it in rather than keep it outside.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{admittere}: \textbf{ad-}, towards, plus \textbf{mittere}, \textbf{to send}.

You have met \emph{mittere} three times already, and this makes four:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{what the prefix does} \\
\midrule
\textbf{meter} & the bare verb, worn down: put in \\
\textbf{el permiso} & \emph{per-}, sent \textbf{through} \\
\textbf{permitir} & the verb of that noun, let through \\
\textbf{admitir} & \emph{ad-}, sent \textbf{towards} — let in \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So the family is a set of sendings, and the prefix does all the steering. English holds the same shelf: \textbf{admit}, \textbf{permit}, \textbf{submit}, \textbf{transmit}, \textbf{commit}, \textbf{mission} — every one a sending in some direction.

\emph{Meter} is the one that came down through speech, which is why it looks least like the others and is the only one you would use about a box.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item applications are not accepted after the deadline
  \item I admit I was wrong
  \item which of the three verbs you do to a form yourself
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To let in? (\textbf{Admitir}.) What does \emph{mittere} mean? (\textbf{To send}.) Which of its relatives would you use about a box? (\textbf{Meter}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(el plazo, entregar, admitir)]{(el plazo, entregar, admitir) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ES-R458-repaso-plazo}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say all three: \emph{the deadline}, \emph{to hand in}, \emph{to let in}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the three of them are one sentence}]
Put them in the order they happen and you have the whole of official life:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Entregue} la solicitud dentro del \textbf{plazo}. Fuera de plazo no se \textbf{admiten}.
\end{quote}

You hand it in, there is a window, and the office decides. Three words, and every form you meet in Spanish will use at least two of them.

Note \emph{dentro del plazo} against \emph{fuera de plazo}: the first takes an article, the second does not, because \emph{fuera de} + bare noun is the fixed frame you met in \emph{fuera de servicio}.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: mittere, for the third time}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{the prefix, and what it does} \\
\midrule
meter & none — put in \\
el permiso & \emph{per-}, sent through \\
admitir & \emph{ad-}, sent towards, let in \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

One Latin verb, three Spanish words, and the prefix is the whole difference. \emph{Meter} came down through speech and looks least like the others; \emph{permiso} and \emph{admitir} were lifted off the page and kept their shape — the same split you saw in \emph{rueda} against \emph{rotativo}.

And \textbf{entregar} hides a different picture: \emph{integrare}, to make whole, so what you hand over should arrive entire.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item hand the form in within the deadline
  \item late applications are not accepted
  \item which of the three has a cart nowhere near it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
All three again, in Spanish, without looking. Then one sentence about a form that arrived too late.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{(la convocatoria) — read it, then do it yourself}

\label{lesson:ES-C458-sintesis-plazo}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{el plazo} and \textbf{admitir}. The notice below puts one against the other in a single line.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
A notice on a noticeboard. Read it, then answer.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{CURSOS DE NATACIÓN — INSCRIPCIÓN}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Plazo}: del 2 al 20 de septiembre.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Entregue} la ficha en el mostrador o por correo.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Fuera de plazo no se \textbf{admiten} fichas, aunque queden plazas.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Listas de admitidos: el día 25.
\end{quote}

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the two ways of handing the form in
  \item what happens if you are a day late
  \item when you find out
\end{itemize}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{Aunque queden plazas} is the hard line, and it is where the grammar earns its keep: \emph{aunque} with the subjunctive — \emph{queden}, not \emph{quedan} — says the office is not conceding that there are places. Had it written \emph{aunque quedan plazas} it would have been admitting there are some and refusing anyway, which reads as spite rather than procedure.

So the subjunctive is doing something worth having: it lets a notice state a rule without commenting on the facts.

Then \textbf{no se admiten} again, with nobody named. Compare the three verbs in their natural order: \emph{usted entrega}, \emph{la oficina admite}, and you would \emph{aceptar} only what is offered to you. The notice never says who decides, because in official Spanish the decision is a thing that happens rather than a person who acts.
\end{culture}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Now your turn, out loud and then in writing. Four lines for a sign-up notice: give the window of dates, say where to hand the form in, say late forms are not accepted, and say when the list goes up.

Then check yourself: did you use \emph{entregar} for the handing in and \emph{admitir} for the office, and did \emph{fuera de plazo} go without an article?
\end{tcolorbox}
